job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Chloe Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my dad in the house I grew up in, in Marsden, a small town about forty minutes from the city. I get up early, print the day's job listings and go through them with a pen, because I think better on paper. Then I send applications to councils, surveying firms and the water company. I finished civil engineering seven months ago, top of my year, and my final project was a flood wall design for a river crossing near our town. I interned with a surveying firm, Hale and Dunn, and on a council road scheme. My mum moved away when I was twelve, so it's just Dad and me, and he drives a bin lorry for the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because I never saw what the fuss was about. I'd tell friends that engineering still needs people who can read a site, not just a screen. I don't post online, so it would be a chat over a cup of tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, which for me means a slow hunt for a first job. I've had 55 applications and three interviews. Civil firms are cautious right now, and my savings are about two months of expenses. I'm not panicking, but I'm counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying and I'd go to the local institution's evening talks to meet people, even though I hate small talk. I'd ask Mr Dunn from the surveying firm if there's anything on a temporary basis. I'd also take a weekend job at the garden centre to cover my share of the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tight, like a collar that's slightly too small. Not painful, but I notice it all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said civil firms are cautious. What are they cautious about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. Councils are cutting budgets, and big schemes are being delayed. If the council doesn't build, the consultants don't hire, and the surveyors lose work. It's a chain, and I'm at the bottom of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a first job change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean I could pay Dad back for the course books and the rent I haven't paid, though he'd never ask. And I'd stop feeling like a guest in my own house. He doesn't make me feel it, but I do.

I'd keep opinions to a **cup of tea**, since I don't post online.

Ask Mr Dunn for any **temporary work** at the surveying firm.

fieldNote: Chloe is **cautious** and reads the market as a chain of council budgets.

steps.text: Print the job listings each morning and send three applications
Ask Mr Dunn for temporary work at the surveying firm
Work Saturdays at the garden centre to cover my bills share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds sensible for office work, but I don't see a computer surveying a riverbank. I'd tell friends to be careful about believing the sales pitch. Some of the claims sound like what they said about driverless cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drawing, calculations and reports are a lot of what a junior does in the first years. If tools do those, a firm needs fewer of us, and the ones it keeps are the ones who can already do the site work. I haven't used any of these tools, and I'm not sure I want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push harder on site-based roles, the ones with boots and a hard hat. I'd also sit down with a friend who uses the tools and see what they actually do, because I'd rather judge it with my own eyes. And I'd ask Dad if the council has any trainee roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary. It's the feeling you get when someone says there's nothing to worry about and then lowers their voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure you want to use the tools. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust what I can't check, and in engineering a wrong number can undermine a bridge. If I can't see how a result was made, I can't sign my name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that put you at a disadvantage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Graduates who use them are faster, and firms like fast. I'd have to learn, but on my terms, slowly, and only for jobs where I can check the answer by hand.

I'd tell friends to **be careful** believing it for site work.

fieldNote: Chloe's resistance is tied to **accountability**: she must be able to check a result by hand.

steps.text: Apply for site engineer and technician roles with contractors
Watch a friend run a design check with AI and compare by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too fast for anyone to behave sensibly. I'd say the government needs to slow things down or at least say what happens to workers. I'd tell friends to keep their heads and not give up on their trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my degree takes a real hit. Even if robots in the field are three years behind, nobody hires a junior when AI can do the drawings. I'd be applying for jobs that don't exist by the time I get an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever steady work is offered, including a trainee surveyor job, since it's hands-on. I'd cut every extra: no new phone, no train trips. I'd ask Dad if I can stay as long as it takes, and I'd help him with the bills in return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying shopping up four flights of stairs and finding out there's another flight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does heavy look like on an ordinary day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wake up at five and not get back to sleep. I'd make Dad's tea, check the listings, and feel guilty for being in the house. By noon I'd be tired and trying to hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd work whatever hours I had to and we'd manage. He'd say we always have. He's not a talker, but he says it with his whole face, and that helps more than advice.

say: I'd say the government must **slow things down** or at least say what happens to workers.
I'd tell friends to keep their heads and not give up their **trades**.
think: My degree takes a **real hit**, and the jobs may be gone by my first interview.
Robots lag three years, so **hands-on** work is where I'd go.

feel: **Heavy**, like finding another flight of stairs with the shopping.
S2.quote: I'd be applying for jobs that don't exist by the time I get an interview.
fieldNote: Chloe turns to **hands-on** work almost immediately and accepts a step down.
Guilt about living at home shows in her **sleep** and mornings.

steps.text: Apply for trainee surveyor jobs, which are hands-on
Stop buying a new phone and cut train trips

Wait two months before spending on any course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to get a foot on a ladder. I'd say let's not panic, but let's be smart. I'd tell friends to look at where robots will take longest, because that's where the safe jobs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get one decent shot. If I land a hands-on job this year, I'd have five years of site experience before the thinking work is done by machines. Then I'd have the one thing a machine can't fake yet: that I've stood on the ground and seen it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first site job and stay in it. I'd study for my chartered exam, which is long and boring but worth it. I'd save about a quarter of every pay cheque. And I'd learn the AI tools, slowly, once I'm earning, because I'd have to by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than I expected. A bit like when the rain slows from heavy to a drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools once you're earning. Why then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd have something to check them against. If I've done twenty site visits and know what a good ground report looks like, I can judge the output. As a fresh graduate with no basis, I'd be trusting blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the council froze all hiring, or if my firm closed. I've seen it in Marsden. Small towns are fragile, and I've seen half a street go when the cement works shut.

say: I'd say **don't panic, be smart**, and look at where robots arrive last.
I'd tell friends the safe jobs are the **hands-on** ones.

I'd learn the tools once I have **check them against**.

steps.text: Take the first site engineering job and stay at least two years

Save a quarter of every pay cheque
Learn the AI tools slowly once I can check results by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is the one where I'd say we'll cope. I'd tell friends to enjoy their twenties and not live in dread. I'd also say the council should publish a plan, so the town isn't left guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, I think. Ten years is enough to be a chartered engineer and have a decade of site work. The jobs will change, but a lot of civil work is slow by nature: permits, weather, access, materials. That slows the machines too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in the next six months and study for my chartered status. I'd rent a place near the town centre within two years and help Dad get a better pension plan. I'd also start learning the tools properly in year three, when I could judge them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'd still have my days of worry, but they'd be ordinary worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the 'ordinary worries'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, my first mortgage, whether Dad's back holds up. Normal things. They're the same ones I'd have with or without any AI, and they'd be the biggest ones in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would you check on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Jess, who studied graphic design. She has less to stand on than I do, and her field is hit first. I'd want to help her find work, even if I can't offer her much.

I'd ask the council to publish a **plan** so the town isn't left guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My degree would lose its use before I'd used it. What would help is a clear plan from the government, trainee jobs on the council that don't need experience, and someone saying plainly what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as slow as I sound. I'm careful because I've seen what happens when people rush in a small town. I'd like someone to give me a chance to show it.

headlineQuote: I'd like someone to give me a chance to show it.
portrait: Chloe is a 23-year-old **civil engineering** graduate, top of her year, living with her father in the small town of Marsden.
She has had 55 applications and three interviews, with about **two months** of savings and a loan.
She is a pragmatic centrist, careful and paper-minded, who never uses AI tools and distrusts anything she can't **check**.
She leans on hands-on and site work, since robots arrive later there, and would learn AI slowly once she can judge it.
Her main stress is feeling like a **guest** at her father's and fearing a small town that could close its jobs.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture worries her most, since her degree and her small town would both be exposed.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a clear **government plan**, trainee council jobs that need no experience, and a plain account of what is coming.
